annotation text 0: This first painting in Hogarth's election series is entitled 'An Election Entertainment'. One party has gathered their supporters in an inn, where they are providing a lavish dinner in the hope of securing voters' support in the coming election. Hogarth's paintings aren't the same thing as realistic photographs - he is a satirist who uses exaggeration, parody and humour. But the paintings do show how a range of people were able to take part in eighteenth-century elections - in different ways - including people who couldn't vote: non-elite men, women, and children. Read on to find out more about these 'entertainments'. Or explore the rest of the painting by zooming in, clicking on other annotations, or listen to what the characters themselves have to say ....
annotation text 1: Election entertainments — or treats — were expected components of eighteenth-century elections. They were (often  excessively alcoholic) dinners given by the candidate(s), either in their country houses or in local taverns, and were intended to flatter supporters and woo potential voters.
annotation text 2:
Hogarth satirizes a tavern-based entertainment in this image — and by implication the process of securing votes through flattering and feasting — as messy, unappealing and generally rather sordid. The gluttonous and drunken collection of voters are shown near the end of the feast provided by the two New Interest Whig candidates, a stylish young man in blue, and an older, more soberly dressed man in brown behind him. Both are seated under the orange New Interest Whig flag at the end of the table. 
Election entertainments like this were exercises in social inversion, as elite male candidates were required to step out of their social sphere and make a show of their willingness to dine and drink with lower-class voters. Both candidates in the image look like they would prefer to be elsewhere. The older candidate is having to endure unwanted handling by, and conversation with, drunken potential voters, while the younger candidate is being forced to accept a kiss from a voter’s wife while the voter’s daughter examines the ring on his hand (or is perhaps contemplating purloining it).
annotation text 3:
Candidates often complained about the need to dine repeatedly with groups of voters and sometimes their womenfolk during hotly contested elections. In part this was because they did not enjoy having to mix, seemingly as equals, with lower-class voters in order to secure their votes, but they also complained about the cost of treating and the heavy drinking culture that accompanied treats. 

A letter to Jackson’s Oxford Journal on 1 June 1753, complained of the drunkenness resulting from one of the treats hosted by Lady Susan Keck and her husband in the lead-up to the Great Oxfordshire Election of 1754: ‘Much less would I have Ladies of Distinction, out of an intemperate Zeal for their Country, send away from their Houses, not only Men, but even Persons of their own Sex, so disguised with Liquor as to merit the Stocks as an Example.’

But Lady Susan knew that treating secured votes; consequently, she started treating long before the election. When she learned in August 1753, nine months before the election, that Lord Wenman, one of the Old Interest Tory candidates, was not treating, she was astonished: ‘Lord Wenman’s own conduct is very incomprehensible since no man that meant to be chosen Beadle, wou’d Lock up his House, and himself, while the thing was depending, therefore all these things consider’d at one view, can only arise from the highest pitch of Idiotism, and Ignorance of the effects of appearances, on the Multitude’ (Bray Papers, Exeter College, 21 Aug. 1753). She continued to treat throughout the campaign and regularly reminded her correspondents that out-treating the Old Interest Tories would be remembered on the hustings: ‘Should Sir James [Sir James Dashwood, one of the Old Interest candidates] come into Oxford or any of the Gang they must always be faced, out eat, out drank, and outdone. At the expence be what it will Command me’ (Bray Papers, Exeter College, 21 Aug. ?Dec. 1753).

verbal description of hotspot location: Top-middle, maybe on the central ceiling beam or above the window.
annotation text 0: Hogarth’s election series paintings were spawned by what has become known as the ‘Great Oxfordshire Election’ of 1754. This extremely long and expensive battle for control of the county (reputedly costing each side £20,000) took place between the New Interest Whigs and the Old Interest Tories. Campaigning began early in 1753 and was carried on with increasing vigour and rancour until the election in April 1754. Even then the outcome of the election remained undecided and was challenged all the way to Parliament. Only after a six-month investigation of witnesses by the Whig-dominated House of Commons were the Old Interest Tory ‘winners’ ousted in April 1755 and the New Interest Whig candidates finally seated.
annotation text 1:
The Oxfordshire election captured widespread public attention, not only because the campaign lasted so long and was so expensive, but also because it involved notable characters, such as the New Interest’s most energetic organiser and campaigner, Lady Susan Keck, and the leading Old Interest Tory candidate, Sir James Dashwood (better known for his leadership of the Hellfire Club). 
Eighteenth-century Oxford University had historically been more Tory than Whig, but by the middle of the century there were deep political divides between colleges. While some academics, like the satirist Dr William King, Principal of St Mary Hall, remained more Jacobite than Tory (he still was a supporter of the previous Stuart monarchy), others, such as Revd Thomas Bray of the leading Whig college, Exeter, was one of the New Interest Whigs’ most active agents and hack writers. With the University ensuring that there was no shortage of men eager to write for either side, the election spawned a paper war. It generated a veritable a blizzard of political poems, songs, pamphlets, satires and squibs. It also saw the founding of the local newspaper, Jackson’s Oxford Journal. As a result, it was widely publicized, providing good copy for London and provincial newspapers.
annotation text 2:
The Tory/Whig battle that dominated the Oxfordshire election was largely backwards-looking by the 1750s. It was the last gasp of a political party struggle that had dominated the first two decades of the century. Neither the Tories nor the Whigs in the eighteenth-century were parties as we know them today, with party structures, registered members and specific political platforms. They were more fluid. 

The Tories had been at their strongest in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth century. They were landed and strongly pro-monarchy, with some Tories being actual Jacobites who believed in divine right of succession, opposed the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the accession of William and Mary to the throne, and remained committed, actively or passively, to the Jacobite cause and the restoration of the Stuart kings. They were also strong supporters of the established Anglican church and against the extension of religious toleration to Protestant Dissenters. 

The Whigs, who were parliamentarians and supporters of constitutional monarchy, had been instrumental in the removal of the Stuart monarchy during the Glorious Revolution and the appointment of William and Mary to the throne thereafter. They supported extension of religious toleration to Protestant Dissenters and had links to the new men and the new wealth being generated by the City of London. 

The Whigs had benefited politically from the accession of George I in 1714. The new king’s experiences with Tory politicians before coming to the throne had led to deep mistrust. Their ambiguous commitment to the Hanoverian Succession and his kingship was compounded by his belief in their latent, if not always active, Jacobitism. As a result, when he came to the throne he proscribed (banned) Tories from court and court positions, and had them removed from political appointments. 

The combination of this proscription, followed by the passage of the Septennial Act in 1716, which extended the length of parliamentary term to seven years (from the previous three), had effectively installed the Whigs at the levers of political power. By the middle of the century therefore, the Tories were largely a spent political force, though with pockets of support in various parts of the country. 

Oxfordshire was one of these. The battle for the county in 1754 saw local grandees (the duke of Marlborough, Lord Macclesfield and Lady Susan Keck), all committed Whigs with connections to the Whig government in Westminster, sponsor local Whig candidates against the (also local) Tory candidates. In addition to the usual parodies and attacks on candidates’ characters, the Whig campaigners made good use of older stereotypes about Tories — they charged the Tory candidates with incipient disloyalty, intimating that they had Jacobite and pro-Catholic sympathies.

For more information on the Oxfordshire election of 1754, see the case study and pollbook for the election https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/case-study-constituencies/oxfordshire/election/Apr-1754/  

For further information on Lady Susan Keck’s involvement in the election, see here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/woman-as-voters-and-participants-in-elections/

verbal description of hotspot location: on flag
annotation text 0: Eighteenth-century elections were colourful affairs. In the Oxfordshire Election of 1754 (on which Hogarth based these paintings) the New Interest Whigs used the colour orange (while the Old Interest Tories were blue). This orange flag has a New Interest slogan on it: 'Liberty and Loyalty'.
annotation text 1: The use of specific colours gave candidates and their supporters a collective visual identity. It made them easy to identify in election processions and in crowds at the hustings. If you look around the room you will see that even people who couldn’t vote in the election could make their preferences known by wearing their candidates’ colours. Here, the female fiddler, the young lady at the back of the picture, and the voter’s wife (the woman kissing the candidate), are all wearing cockades in New Interest colours.
annotation text 2: Although Tory candidates were increasingly being represented by blue — ‘true blue’ — in the eighteenth-century, eighteenth-century candidates were free to select whatever colour they wanted. Often they chose to use the colour that their family already used for their racehorses.
annotation text 3: For an example of an 18th century cockade: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/91453630-62ff-4fb0-9a00-8bb76a304356/.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the pile of cockades on the table, bottom-left.
annotation text 0: Cockades are made of ribbon, knotted together. They came in distinctive colours, showing political allegiance. This pile of cockades are orange, the colour of the Oxfordshire New Interest Whigs in 1754. Others, already pinned to hats, lie ready for distribution under the table.
annotation text 1: Cockades were made of coloured ribbon by local tailors and dressmakers, or by candidates’ wives, daughters and servants, or even by voters themselves. They might be in one colour, as they are here, representing the New Interest, or in separate colours to show support for two candidates who were running together. Cockades were worn pinned to hats, clothes, and even used to decorate horses’ harnesses.
annotation text 2:
Sometimes cockades were given out carefully, one per (male) voter; at other times, they were worn by men, women and children not entitled to vote.
Few eighteenth-century politicians understood the value of campaigning literature and the use of political symbols better than the radical John Wilkes, so it is not surprising that cockades featured in the detailed instructions he issued to his voters during the Middlesex elections of 1768. Not only did he use the press to ensure that his supporters knew just how many coaches would be available to take them to vote at Brentford, and where to find them, but he also deliberately specified that each supporter would be issued with a blue cockade and a card bearing the slogan “Liberty and Wilkes”, neither of which the freeholders were supposed to use until that morning. (Public Advertiser, 31 Mar. 1768).
annotation text 3:
The purchase of ribbons for cockades was a significant election expense for candidates, as ribbons were hand-woven and costly, and much ribbon would be required for cockades in heated election contests. These coloured ribbons gave candidates and their supporters a collective visual identity and made them easy to identify in election processions and in crowds at the hustings. They were believed to be so costly and influential that an act was passed in 1826/7 — 1826–27 (367) 7/8 Geo. IV. Sess. 1826/7 — to prohibit  candidates or their agents from giving voters and non-voters ‘any cockade, ribbon or other mark of distinction’. The proposed fine was steep at £10 per cockade or ribbon given out, but whether anyone was actually ever charged with doing so is debatable.

For a discussion in the House of Commons regarding the importance of ribbons to silk weavers’ livelihoods, resulting from silk weavers’ petitions to Parliament in 1828, requesting that the prohibition on ribbons and cockades in elections be repealed, see here: Hansard, ‘Election Expenses — Use of Ribbons’, 20 Mar. 1828: https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/1828-03-20/debates/566a5f74-d6c4-4c9e-84f9-a5066afb1f16/ElectionExpenses%E2%80%94UseOfRibbons#:~:text=The%20bill%20itself%20he%20considered,respecting%20the%20use%20of%20ribbons.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the Whig candidate (young man in blue)
annotation text 0: The stylishly dressed young Whig candidate, Sir Commodity Taxem, looks out pleadingly to the viewer, while a voter wearing a coachman’s wig pushes his wife forward for a kiss.
annotation text 1: In this image, Hogarth is satirizing a common eightenenth-century election practice: kissing for votes. Although it seems rather odd to us now, it was taken for granted among eighteenth-century politicians, canvassers and satirists that voters’ wives had influence over, and at times even controlled, their husbands’ votes. Consequently, kissing voters’ wives and/or daughters was customary practice for candidates; so too was providing wives and daughters with gifts of various sorts.
annotation text 2:
The electioneering kiss served a number of purposes: it demonstrated the approachability and genuine politeness of the candidate (or whoever was canvassing for him), by showing that he was willing to step out of his class and kiss women who were not his social equals; it flattered the voters’ sense of self-importance; and, finally, it was intended to create a sense of obligation in the woman and/or her husband, and secure votes. 
Among elite men and women it was usually depicted as one of the distasteful but necessary duties that came with being politically active and maintaining a political interest. Thus, Lord Dartford saw it as a suitable penance for Lord North when North went dutifully to his borough of Banbury in August 1766 instead paying him a visit: ‘I hope for his punishment he will spend all this delightful weather in eating Venison in Banbury, and kissing the Aldermen’s Ladies’ (Bodleian Library, MS North d.10, fo. 171v, Dartmouth to Guilford, Sandwell, 22 Aug. 1766). 

Alderman’s ladies were conventionally described as vulgar and unappealing, but they were at least higher on the social ladder than freeholders’ wives, who were often depicted as loathsome. Hogarth here is suggesting that this woman is a voter’s wife. The idea that candidates were expected to kiss either group of women, or to be kissed by them, provided satirists like Hogarth with copy.
annotation text 3: On the history of the kiss in eighteenth-century elections see https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/kisses-for-votes/

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above banner stating 'Give us our Eleven Days', on the floor at the bottom of the painting.
annotation text 0: By the eighteenth century the Julian calendar, which was still in use in Britain, was a full eleven days out of sync with the Gregorian calendar, which was used in most of the rest of Europe. In 1752 (two years before Hogarth began this painting), the Whig government decreed that the country should fully adopt of the Gregorian calendar. It was not a universally popular decision, and when Wednesday 2 September 1752 was followed by Thursday 14 September, there was some dissent (although probably not full-scale rioting, as has sometimes been supposed). The blue banner that the injured Whig bruiser  — reputedly a well-known Oxford fighter named Teague Carter —  has captured from the Tories reads, ‘Give us our eleven days’. Hogarth is using this popular slogan to comment bitingly on the intensity, and foolishness, of the political beliefs circulating at the time of this election.
annotation text 1:
Although the Calendar Reform bill passed through parliament easily, and the change was widely publicised and explained by the government, it was highly unpopular. For some, it was seen as inherently un-British, a change that had been brought in to conform to 'Popish' (i.e. Catholic) European practice; for yet others, it was more threatening, as they might be losing days of rental income, or perhaps even genuinely believed that the government was depriving them of eleven days of their lives.
Hogarth’s inclusion of this slogan on a Tory banner references the recent calendar reform riots and satirizes the ignorance of the crowd. It also — and more specifically with relation to the Oxfordshire election in 1754 — highlights the Old Interest Tory use of calendar reform as a way of attacking the New Interest Whigs, particularly Thomas Parker, the young New Interest Whig candidate. 
Parker was the son and heir of the local Whig grandee, George Parker, 2nd earl of Macclesfield. Macclesfield and the duke of Marlborough were the two local aristocrats directing the New Interest Whig campaign. Both had close ties to the Whig government but Macclesfield, in particular, had been a driving force in securing the passage of calendar reform through parliament. Protesting against calendar reform in Oxfordshire was therefore yet another a way of intimating that the Whig government had overseen an attack on individual rights and freedoms.
annotation text 2: Parties employed 'stavesmen' or 'bludgeon-men' to protect their candidates and supporters, and perhaps to disrupt or even attack their opponents.  For an actual eighteenth-century bludgeon of the sort used by election enforcers, see here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/31257118-e5d8-417c-ab51-626a2006aaa9/

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the blue 'Marry and Multiply' banner visible thorugh the window
annotation text 0: The Old Interest Tories parading outside the window carry banners, one of which reads ‘Liberty’ and another ‘Marry and Multiply in Spite of the Devil’. The two banners form a protest against Hardwicke’s Marriage Act of 1753, which had only come into effect in a month before the 1754 election.
annotation text 1: After the passage of Hardwicke’s Marriage Act, legal marriages had to meet the following criteria: (i) young men or women under the age of twenty-one could only marry with the formal consent of their parents or guardians (in spite of the fact that the age of consent remained 12 for girls and 14 for boys); (ii) all weddings had to take place between 08.00 and 12.00 — thus the development of the ‘wedding breakfast’; this was to prevent late-night clandestine marriages fuelled by alcohol; (iii) couples who wanted to marry in private had to apply for and obtain a special licence; (iv) all other couples had to marry in public in their (Anglican) parish church, but only after the minister had formally announced their forthcoming marriage during Sunday service (known as reading the banns) for the three previous weeks; (v) all marriages had to be formally registered and recorded; they had to include the signatures of the minister, the bride and groom, and two witnesses (this aimed to prevent the possibility of bigamy).
annotation text 2: Hardwicke’s Marriage act was one of the most divisive pieces of legislation of the eighteenth century because it was popularly believed to be an attack on individual liberty in choice of marriage partner. Just what constituted a formal, legal marriage had become very confused over the centuries, so this Act clarified and tightened up the law for England and Wales. Its main aim was to make clandestine marriages illegal — clandestine marriages were irregular, often secret, marriages, usually carried out by impoverished or rogue clergymen and poorly recorded, or not recorded at all. Propertied fathers — such as the MPs — were worried that their heirs or heiresses might be seduced into clandestine marriages, or just marry against family wishes, and the family’s property and wealth would pass on to social inferiors or adventurers. By giving parents a veto over the marriage of children under the age of twenty-one, the Act created widespread anger, as it was interpreted as removing young people’s liberty to choose who to marry, or to marry for love.

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above the effigy seen through the window
annotation text 0: The Old Interest Tory mob is parading an antisemitic effigy with stereotypically Jewish features, which bears a placard that reads ‘No Jews’. Hogarth is referring here to the way that the shortlived Jewish Naturalisation Act (passed by the Whig government in July 1753 and repealed that December) became a ‘seismic’ issue in the election of 1754.
annotation text 1: The actual purpose of the Jewish Naturalisation Act was simple: it made possible the naturalisation of a small number of foreign-born Jewish people (there were only about 7,000–8,000 Jewish families in total in the country at the time, many of whom were British by birth, and most of whom lived in London or Bristol). Nor would naturalisation would have granted these few foreign-born Jews full citizenship; they, like British-born Jews and Roman Catholics, would still have been subject to legal discrimination and have been unable to vote or hold government office or appointments.
annotation text 2:
The passage of the Jewish Naturalisation Act led to rumours of Whig corruption that were fed by deep-seated, historic, antisemitic beliefs, and were picked up and disseminated by the press, particularly Jackson’s Oxford Journal and the London Evening Post. 
Tory rumours charged the Whig government (falsely) with corruption, suggesting that the Prime Minister and his brother had been bribed into putting forward the legislation by rich Jewish businessmen. Opportunistic politicians, clergymen and hack writers fed the rumours, dredged up antisemitic slurs and fed fears of a Jewish take-over of English culture and society, a conspiracy theory not unlike those circulating today.

 The act was used politically to whip up popular fear and anger, with the result that  mobs threatened riots and violence against Whig candidates and their supporters. This was particularly the case in Oxfordshire where the rumours and conspiracies were tacitly supported by Sir James Dashwood, one of the Old Interest Tory candidates. The popular opposition to the act was so great that the Whig government repealed the act after only five months.
annotation title: Protest against the Jewish Naturalization Act

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above the chafing dish on the table.
annotation text 0: A corpulent, sweating parson has removed his wig and (having apparently already stripped a ham bone bare) is about to eat a further dish being cooked on a chafing dish. These were metal pans used for cooking food at the table.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the escutcheon on the wall
annotation text 0: The central section of a coat of arms (the ‘escutcheon’) is hanging on the wall. When Hogarth made an engraving of his painting, he added details, including the specific identification of this coat of arms as belonging to a venal ‘Elector’, whose vote is for sale to the highest bidder. The escutcheon bears a chevron between three guineas, the engraving adding a gaping mouth  as a crest, and the motto 'Speak and Have’ below.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the lobster
annotation text 0: The lobster, along with other foodstuffs, jug and pewter plates, forms a miniature still life painting in the midst of the larger image. These details are symbolic of the greed and gluttony of the voters and the costly extravagance and wastefulness of the election feast (especially since these items seem to have fallen from the overset table).
annotation text 1: This section of the painting is also a reference to popular contemporary Dutch still-life paintings of luxurious fruits, flowers, fish and fowl, displayed ostentatiously. As such, it is also a small pointed reminder to Hogarth's viewers that he saw himself as (and also was) a serious painter, as well as a popular caricaturist and moral critic.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the brick being thrown
annotation text 0: Several bricks and other objects have been thrown through the window by the Old Interest Tory supporters. One is smashing the tavern window, and another has hit the Whig election agent on the heand. This represents the threat - and often the actuality - of violence in eighteenth-century elections.
annotation text 1:
Emotions often ran high in 18th century elections. They were rumbustious affairs and it was not unusual for fights, or even riots to break out between the supporters of the different candidates. Deaths due to election violence were sadly not uncommon.
The protest outside the Whigs’ election entertainment comes from a Tory mob which is attempting to break in to the inn. The Tory supporters, wearing blue cockades, are carrying banners and parading an effigy. They are throwing bricks through the window and wielding bludgeons. A man inside the inn is emptying a chamber pot full of urine over them. On the right of the painting, a group of orange-cockaded Whig stavesmen are enthusiastically using their weapons to counter another attempt to enter the room.
annotation text 2: For further information on violence and rioting in eighteenth-century elections, see: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/violence-and-riot/

verbal description of hotspot location: on barrel of punch
annotation text 0: In placing the young serving boy making a huge half-barrel full of punch at the front of the image, Hogarth is foregrounding the alcoholic excess that was a common feature of election entertainments. He is also criticising the luxury and expense of elections, as punch was a costly elite drink at the time whose key ingredients — lemons; sugar; rum, brandy or arrack (a distilled alcohol made from sugarcane); and nutmeg — were expensive imports from various parts of the British empire.
annotation text 1: Floating in the punch is a punch bowl made of china. Punch was customarily drunk from such vessels (as Hogarth depicted in his frequently engraved painting 'A Midnight Modern Conversation'), an indication that it was a drink usually enjoyed by high-status men. That the small, delicately patterned bowl is disused, while the punch is being mixed in a huge vat (which has to be repenished) is a comment on the way in which elections allow a broader cross-section of the population to participate in practices normally the preserve of the elite, but with the politer elements of those practices getting lost in the process.

verbal description of hotspot location: Near the scabbard on the bench
annotation text 0: The gloves and scabbard on the bench, and discarded cutlery on the table, indicate that another diner was recently sitting here. He is presumably now defending the room against the Tory supporters trying to get in: we see him at the right of the painting, wielding the sword just taken from its scabbard.

verbal description of hotspot location: on gloves/stockings on the table, bottom-left.
annotation text 0: The gloves and stockings on the table have been provided for the candidates by a Quaker, identified in Hogarth's engraving of this painting as Abel Squat. They are  'Presents for each Voter’s Lady’ that will be given to the exclusively male voters to secure their wives’ or daughters’ influence. Hogarth is calling attention to this kind of low-level bribery, which was not at all unusual in elections, as part of his all-encompassing criticism of electoral corruption. Abel Squat holds a promissory note signed 'R Pention’ promising to pay £20 in six months time, presuambly to cover the cost of the stockings and gloves. The candidates are evidently paying for the election on credit.
annotation text 1: Candidates’ gifts were intended to flatter the voters and their families, and secure votes. Voting was a transactional affair in the eighteenth-century and many voters expected to get something in return for the ‘property’ of their votes. While gifts of money might be seen as bribery, material goods were regarded as more acceptable, and were calibrated to the social status of the voter. They could range from simple twists of tobacco through to small items of clothing or accessories (for instance gloves, stockings, handkerchiefs) for labouring- and middling-class freeholders, to luxuries for gentry voters such as hot-house-grown grapes and pineapples, or gifts of fish or game (such as trout, pheasant or venison).
annotation text 2:
As voters’ womenfolk, especially their wives, were believed to exercise substantial influence over their their menfolk’s votes, candidates often made efforts to flatter women with gifts of material goods. This could include ribbons in party colours, cloth for new dresses (also perhaps in party colours), or pieces of lace to trim clothing. 'Birds of a Feather all Flock Together', a poem from the Durham election of 1813, focuses on George Baker’s method of canvassing the ladies: he not only gives them a special election treat, ‘… with plenty / Of Meat, Drink, and Fruit, and every thing dainty’ — but also gives them ‘Dresses alike’ of ‘Lincoln Green’ — to secure their support.
Charles Dickens, in 'The Pickwick Papers' (1836) reflects the longevity of this practice in his comedic sketch of the fictional Eatanswill election. At Eatanswill, the candidate purchases female support respectably (as opposed to corruptly) by flattering the women’s sense of social importance and appealing to their vanity and love of luxury. At the end of a special tea party, given for the women, each woman is given the parting gift of an expensive and highly fashionable parasol in the candidate’s colours. As he proudly explains to Mr Pickwick, it may have been expensive, but it was worth it: ‘Fact, my dear Sir, fact. Five-and-forty green parasols, at seven and sixpence a-piece. All women like finery, — extraordinary the effect of those parasols. Secured all their husbands, and half their brothers — beats stockings, and flannel, and all that sort of thing hollow. My idea, my dear Sir, entirely. Hail, rain, or sunshine, you can’t walk half a dozen yards up the street, without encountering half a dozen green parasols.’

verbal description of hotspot location: on/near the musicians
annotation text 0: Hogarth portrays four musicians who play an odd combination of instruments. The woman playing the violin (or fiddle) would have been recognised by some eighteenth-century contemporaries as ‘Fiddling Nan’, a popular Oxfordshire musician. The other musicians are not identifiable; nor do they seem to be playing at the moment captured in the painting. The rather arrogant-looking man holding the bass viol is staring at a bottle of burgundy wine on the table, presumably hoping to secure a drink. Next to him is a man holding his instrument (possibly a viola da gamba) while drinking and having his long chin tweaked by an aristocrat dressed in grey trimmed with gold lacing; the final musician, a rough-looking fellow wearing a tam, is presented as a stereotyped Scotsman, complete with bagpipes. He has stopped playing to scratch at lice.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the pollbook
annotation text 0: This lawyer, who is acting as Secretary or agent for the election committee, has been struck on the head with a brick while examining or writing in what is probably an old pollbook (recording how constituents voted in a previous elections), now being used as a canvassing book (recording their voting intentions for the new election). He has been using some blank pages to list ‘Sure Votes’ — of which there is only one thus far — and ‘Doubtful Votes’, of which there are significantly more. (Curiously, in Hogarth's print of the painting, the 'Sure Votes' page is full, and the 'Doubtful' empty: perhaps Hogarth altered this to show the bribery to have been successful.)
annotation text 1: There was no secret ballot in the eighteenth century. Instead, voters had to declare their votes out loud in front of gathered crowds when they came up to vote. Their names and addresses, and the names of the candidates for whom they voted, were recorded by a polling clerk. Completed pollbooks were then often published and sold by local printers shortly after the election. Candidates, election agents and canvassers frequently used the pollbook from the most recent election as the basis for their canvassing, scribbling on blank pages, or annotating the text as they canvassed voters. While there would undoubtedly have been some deaths and changes in the voterate between elections, having an old pollbook gave canvassers a document to work from.
annotation text 2: The ECPPEC digital resource contains the transcribed and searchable records of all surviving eighteenth-century pollbooks. The Pollbook Directory allows you to search for elections and polling data here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/pollbook-directory/.
annotation title: The election agent and his poll book

verbal description of hotspot location: On the laurel leaves
annotation text 0: Laurel leaves, signifying the hoped-for victory, are attached to the back of each of the two candidates' chairs.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the oil painting on the wall at the left of the painting
annotation text 0: A dimly lit oil painting shows a church and other buildings on fire. Oxford, where Hogarth loosely set his election paintings, had suffered a great fire in 1644. Since this was during the Civil War,  perhaps the painting alludes to the disastrous effects of political conflict. It may alternatively be Hogarth's more general, but still ominous comment on the state of the nation in his own time.

verbal description of hotspot location: Man in red with tongue hanging out, near the candidates
annotation text 0: This man's leather apron indicates he is a cobbler. He is holding the hand of one of the candidates and seems to be toasting him. Another man, with a dislodged wig and dirty or scratched face, is also pestering the candidate, who appears unamused at having to endure the cordiality of his social inferiors.

verbal description of hotspot location: Portrait, top-centre of painting
annotation text 0: The portrait is of King William III (1650-1702), and seems to have been based on an original paitning, often engraved, by Sir Godfrey Kneller. William III took the throne with his wife Mary II in 1688-89 at the time of the so-called 'Glorious Revolution', and so was a hero to the Whigs, who had pushed for this change of dynasty as a means of limiting royal power. The portrait has been defaced by slashing, presumably not by the Whigs, but  by the Old Interest Tories who (it is implied) had used the same room in the tavern previously.

verbal description of hotspot location: Between the three men in brown and the gent. in blue coat, underneath the window.
annotation text 0: Three voters, of different ages, but all dressed as if they have come into town from the countryside, are captivated by a more smartly dressed man who is making a puppet with his hand and a napkin. The puppet mocks the man's neighbour, who appears ill, and whose crutch, stashed behind his chair, indicates he suffers from gout.
annotation text 1: John Nichols, who published anecdotes about his contemporaries, reported that he had been told by Hogarth himself that only one figure in this picture was supposed to represent the likeness of a real person. This was the smartly-dressed man making the hand-puppet, who was based on the Irishman John Parnell, an attorney and friend of Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift.  Hogarth told  Nichols (Nichols claimed) that Parnell had begged the favour of being included in the painting, arguing that he was so well known in Ireland that his appearance in the painting would help the sales of its engravings in Dublin. Nichols also spectulated that other characters in the painting were based on real figures, including the well-dressed candidate, who Nichols said was based on Thomas Potter (?1718-59) MP, an associate of the radical John Wilkes and possibly the author of the scandalous poem 'Essay on Woman'.  ('Biographical Anecdotes of William Hogarth; with a Catalogue of his Works', London: 1785), p.335.)

verbal description of hotspot location: On the mayor passed out having eaten too many oysters
annotation text 0: The mayor, or perhaps an alderman, has eaten so many oysters that he has passed out, or perhaps even died. In an attempt to revive him, he is being 'bled' by a barber-surgeon (although no blood is flowing into the bowl).

verbal description of hotspot location: On the shoulder of the woman in blue, standing at the window at the left
annotation text 0: A solider in a red coat gives or receives a snuff box held by a young lady who is wearing orange New Interest ribbons. The soldier simultaneous shakes hands with a man standing behind her, who is dressed in the robes of an alderman and is probably the woman’s husband. The snuffbox, the woman being between the two men, and the alderman raising his glass above her head, suggest that some kind of transaction is taking place, no doubt connected with the promise of a vote. The woman's feelings about this, and her agency in the transaction, is unclear. Perhaps the alderman has encouraged his wife to persuade the soldier to vote for the New Interest, but the tender expression on the younger people's faces, and the exchange of the gift, suggest that their relationship may be developing further.

verbal description of hotspot location: Prominent location for note marker since this is the introductory annotation. Top-left of painting?
annotation text 0: This second painting in Hogarth's election series is entitled 'Canvassing for Votes'. The setting has moved from the town to a village street with three pubs. We are still during the campaigning phrase of the election, before the voting takes place. The ’canvass’ is the attempt to secure political support by visiting and talking to the voters, and inducing them with gifts and promises.  Press 'Play' to hear what’s going on in this scene, or explore the detail of the painting by clicking on the notes.

verbal description of hotspot location: On/near the canvassers at the centre of the picture
annotation text 0: The landlords of the two opposing taverns — The Royal Oak (nearer to us), which supports the Tory candidate, and The Crown (in the background), which supports the Whig candidate — are canvassing Farmer Rye, a substantial and well-dressed man, for his vote. They are offering him tally tickets, which will give him free food and drink at their taverns, as well as money. His sidelong glance at bewigged landlord of The Crown, who is giving him a large handful of coins, perhaps indicates that the Whigs have succeeded in bribing him.
annotation text 1: While providing voters with free food and drink was an expected (and largely accepted) perk of eighteenth-century elections, the line between treating and bribery was always blurry. Similarly, reimbursing voters for the cost of travel and loss of wages in order to come to vote was usually accepted, but the buying of votes through open payments was not. Candidates, their patrons, or their election committees, hired local taverns, sometimes months in advance of an election, to supply voters who supported them (and often their family members) with free food and drink. In Taunton in 1830, for instance, voters who had promised to vote for one of the candidates were given a tally ticket for 8 quarts of beer. These tickets could be redeemed at any of the candidate’s supporting taverns (and there would be a number of them in a town). This sort of treating with food and drink made elections expensive. It only became illegal and a form of bribery if it took place after the date of the writ —the official document formally calling the election — which was sent from London to all the sheriffs in the counties on the dissolution of the old parliament.
annotation text 2: Eighteenth-century elections were ideally meant to be absolutely free, with all voters able to cast their votes independently. This was not always the case, however; there were a few boroughs where corruption was open and blatant, and where votes were effectively sold to the highest bidder. In most places, canvassers were persistent; they coaxed, treated, and even threatened voters to secure their votes, but managed to stay on the right side of open corruption.  In addition to free food and drink, canvassers might give voters small gifts for themselves or members of their families (such as twists of tobacco, or cloth for a new dress for a wife or child). They might promise to forgive unpaid debts or offer voters, or members of their families, work or patronage in the future. Voters who refused to promise their votes might have more pressure put upon them; they might be threatened with the bailiff and the distraint of their possessions, or have any unpaid rent or debts called in at very short notice. They might even be threatened with the loss of their jobs or future work, or their tenancies. While some voters saw voting as transactional and angled to get the best deal possible (be that in cash or goods or promises) from either party in return for their votes, there were also always others who resisted blandishments and coercion, and voted as they wished. Examples of all of these tactics exist in witness statements given in cases of controverted elections — that is, elections where the outcome was challenged by petitions to parliament and MPs had to determine the outcome of the election after hearing from witnesses on both sides.
annotation text 3: While Hogarth is suggesting that the entire electoral system is corrupt, the line between legitimate treating and canvassing and bare-faced bribery and corruption was indistinct. Candidates who wanted electoral reform and campaigned for the ‘purity’ of elections might demand that all voters take the bribery oath before voting, on the belief that few would dare to vote if they had first to swear to their electoral independence on the Bible.  For further information on Canvassing, see: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/getting-the-vote-out-canvassing/

verbal description of hotspot location: On the Punch banner
annotation text 0: This temporary election banner has been hung in front of the tavern sign for the Royal Oak (the Tory inn). In the lower half, it features the comic and costumed figure of Punch (better known to us today from Punch and Judy puppet shows). Punch, identified at the bottom of the banner as the candidate for the election in the borough of ‘Guzzledown’, is throwing coins to the voters from a wheelbarrow full of money.  The upper half depicts the newly-built Treasury building in Whitehall, London, and shows a shower of gold coins pouring out of a window. They are falling into a sack which will be put onto the coach labelled ‘Oxford’ – a satirical allusion to the cost of the 1754 Oxfordshire election which partly inspired Hogarth’s paintings.
annotation text 1: Hogarth uses Punch and this banner to suggest that cash-for-votes is the Tory strategy for winning the election in ‘Guzzledown’. This bribery, while blatant (and lucrative for the voters), will be carefully disguised, however; in other words, it will be as difficult to pin on the candidate as it would be to identify who was wearing the Punch costume. The figure of ‘Punch’ — a subversive and carnivalesque figure, easily identified by his peaked hat, enormous belly and caricatured humpback — was well-known in eighteenth-century England. It owes its origins to the comic figure of Polichinello in the Italian Commedia del Arte, but would have been better known in England through the popular puppet Punch and Joan (the predecessor to Judy) shows that toured the country. Exactly when the figure of Punch became politicized is uncertain, but we know that it was being used politically in publications from the 1720s.
annotation text 2: Punch’s involvement in eighteenth-century politics was not made up by Hogarth. A man dressed as Punch and a cross-dressed figure of ‘Mrs Punch’ were used to give cash to voters (and often their families) in two outstandingly corrupt elections — the Shaftesbury and Hindon elections of 1774. In both cases, the results of the elections were overturned on charges of bribery and corruption. In the case of Hindon, the bribery was so blatant that the unseated candidates were sentenced to 6 months in prison and fined 1,000 marks (nearly £60,000 in today’s money).
annotation text 3: For more information on ‘Electoral Corruption in the Long Eighteenth Century’, see https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/electoral-corruption-in-the-long-eighteenth-century/

verbal description of hotspot location: On/near the cobbler and barber seated at table on the right
annotation text 0: Two older men are sitting in front of the third inn in the picture, the Porto Bello. One is a barber, with his shaving dish, jug and napkin on the floor near his feet; the other is a cobbler, indicated by his leather apron and the shoe on the table in front of him. Both cobblers and barbers were commonly used to represent politically aware, independent voters in the eighteenth century. As local men in jobs where people tended to gather and chat while they waited, they were ideally placed to hear the news and be vocal critics of the government. Hogarth is suggesting however, that even the cobbler has been ‘bought’ in this election, as he is covering a collection of coins with his hand.
annotation text 1: Hogarth is using recent eighteenth-century naval history to make a political point here that would have been obvious to his contemporaries. The local barber and cobbler are seated in front of the Porto Bello tavern. The inn sign can be made out above the barber’s head and his forefinger points out the name of the inn on his tankard. The cobbler, smoking his pipe and with a shoe on the table beside him, is listening to the barber (presumably an ex-naval barber-surgeon), who is using his pipe to point at a curved line of broken pipe stems. He is recounting — and demonstrating — Admiral Edward Vernon’s successful defeat of the Spanish navy at Portobello in 1739.
annotation text 2: Admiral Edward Vernon was a popular hero, with a well-established reputation for both personal integrity and political independence. Hogarth has drawn on this reputation by placing the Porto Bello inn directly opposite the Tories’ tavern, The Royal Oak, where the corrupt canvassing is taking place. To drive the reference home, he has also included the carved figurehead of the British Lion eating a French fleur-de-lys directly across from the barber’s Porto Bello tankard. This figurehead came from another famous ship, HMS Centurion, in which Admiral Lord Anson circumnavigated the globe in 1744.  Unlike Admiral Vernon, Admiral Lord Anson was a Whig politician and longstanding member of the government. Hogarth is using this representation of his naval achievement to criticize him as a member of the political elite and a member of the government, and to suggest that even achievements of Whigs like Anson could be appropriated politically and tarnished through their proximity to electoral corruption. It is worth noting, though, that in actuality Anson’s leadership of the Royal Navy was crucial to restoring British naval power and securing British naval superiority by mid-century.

verbal description of hotspot location: On/near the lion
annotation text 0: The carved British Lion, which is portrayed eating a French fleur-de-lys, represents the figurehead of a famous ship, Admiral Lord Anson’s HMS Centurion, in which he successfully completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1744. It is placed directly across the picture from the Porto Bello inn and, specifically, opposite the barber who is sitting at the table with his forefinger pointing at the words ‘Porto Bello’ inscribed on his tankard. Admiral Lord Anson was a popular naval hero, but also a political insider, a leading Whig politician and longstanding member of the government (he rose to become First Lord of the Admiralty). Hogarth is using the figurehead to contrast Anson’s insider status against the political independence of another naval hero, the politically independent Admiral Edward Vernon, who was famous for his successful defeat of the Spanish navy at Portobello in 1739.
annotation text 1: The symbolism of the British lion eating a French fleur-de-lys would have also had an additional layer of meaning for eighteenth-century viewers, as, by the time that Hogarth painted this picture, Britain was involved in an imperial struggle against France for territorial control of the Ohio valley in North America (the French and Indian War of 1754–6). This struggle would morph in 1756 into the Seven Years’ War (1756–63), a global conflict that would see Britain fighting France in North America, Europe and India.

verbal description of hotspot location: On The Royal Oak building or sign
annotation text 0: The Royal Oak is one of the three inns represented in this scene. We know by its inn sign that it supports the Tory interest in the election as the oak tree on the sign references the oak that the young Charles II reputedly climbed to avoid capture by Parliamentarian soldiers after the Battle of Worcester in 1651. Hogarth is suggesting that while the Tories support the monarchy and the state, their support is really for the previous Stuart dynasty, which ended with the removal of Charles II’s brother, James II, in the ‘Glorious Revolution’ of 1688-89, and not for the current Hanoverian dynasty, which the Whigs supported.
annotation text 1: The Royal Oak is the most fashionable, substantial and well-kept (and visibly prosperous) inn of the three in the picture. It is offering the supporting voters — two of whom are visible through the downstairs window — meals of roast chicken and enormous meat pies. Tory supporters are also dimly visible through the upstairs window. It is implied that the candidate himself was recently among them – although he is now at street level, he seems to have left his hat on the balcony, where he was presumably talking to the two fashionably-dressed women. The well-dressed landlord of the Royal Oak, wearing a hat, with just the tip of his blue cockade showing over the tip of the brim, is outside canvassing Farmer Rye for the Tories. He is offering a tally ticket for food and drink in the inn, and slipping a coin into the farmer’s hand for his vote. The landlady of the Royal Oak is seated at the door, next to (or on) the British lion. She is counting the proceeds of supporting the Old Interest Tories. Like her husband, she is tidily and fashionably dressed. The blue ribbon on her mob cap and her blue sleeves indicate her support for the Tory candidate.  She is being watched by a grenadier guard, who has perhaps been hired to protect the inn.
annotation text 2: By placing the banner ‘Punch candidate for Guzzledown’ in front of the sign for the Royal Oak, almost obscuring it, Hogarth is suggesting that the election will be won by whoever is able to pay the voters the most for their votes.
annotation title: The Royal Oak, and the Tories

verbal description of hotspot location: The Excise Office/Crown Inn sign
annotation text 0: The sign of The Crown towards the rear of the painting identifies the Whig-supporting inn. While the sign of a crown designates the Whigs’ support for the current Hanoverian monarchy under George II, Hogarth is criticizing the Whigs by having the name The Excise Office hang under the sign. This is a specific reference to the Excise Crisis of 1733, when an extremely unpopular excise (an internal tax) bill was introduced (and later withdrawn) by a previous Whig Prime Minister, Sir Robert Walpole. The sign suggests that the Whigs are all about money.
annotation text 1: The Excise Bill of 1733 proposed to reduce the customs duty paid on two popular imports — tobacco and wine — when they entered the country, and raise revenue for the government instead by having it paid individually by shopkeepers and retailers — who in turn passed the cost on to shoppers. This was in itself very unpopular across the country, but it was the powers of search that the bill would have given to hated excisemen that spawned a petitioning and press campaign, and resulted in the bill’s withdrawal. In the government’s desire to cut down on smuggling and ensure that the excise on goods was paid, it would have granted excisemen not only the right to enter and search private individual’s houses, force open their trunks and cupboards, and reverse the burden of proof. In other words, an exciseman could presume that individuals were guilty of harbouring smuggled goods, or avoiding the excise, and it was up to the individual to prove they were not. It would have overturned the very important English belief in a right to privacy (the common belief that an Englishman’s home was his castle), as well as threatening the fundamental political belief in innocent until proven guilty. As part of his even-handed attack on all parties, Hogarth is bringing all of this together to suggest that the Whigs were all about high taxation, as well as posing a threat to the traditional rights and liberties of the English populace.
annotation title: The Crown inn, and the Whigs

verbal description of hotspot location: Man sawing sign
annotation text 0: The Crown is surrounded by a mob who are attacking it (whether about the election or taxation is not made clear). A well-dressed man in an upper window is trying to disperse the crowd by shooting into it. However, the crowd is in danger of being crushed by the man who is sawing through the inn sign while another pulls it down with a rope. Hogarth’s symbolism here is stark, but equivocal. He is perhaps suggesting that unless the population wakes up to the damage that corruption is doing to the state, the state itself will fall and the people will be crushed. He may also be suggesting that the people’s blind rage against anyone they perceive at harming their immediate interests will do more harm than good. Either way, they are evidently oblivious to the danger they are in.
annotation title: A mob, and an accident waiting to happen

verbal description of hotspot location: On the Peddler just outside the bay window
annotation text 0: Peddlers or hawkers were men and women who travelled around towns and cities or the countryside selling cheap goods, which might range from items of food to printed materials to the kind of miscellaneous trinkets shown in this man's tray. Hogarth represents this peddler as having stereotypically Jewish features. Jews would have comprised only a small proportion of itinerant traders (after all, there were probably fewer than 10,000 Jews in England in the 1750s, most of whom were in London). But the antisemitic trope of the Jewish peddler was commonplace, and was both fed by anti-Jewish sentiments and helped to perpetuate and enforce them. Why Hogarth chose to portray this individual as stereotypically Jewish is not clear, but it is probably related to the Jewish Naturalisation Act in 1753, which had been strongly opposed by Tories such as the candidate shown here making purchases from the peddler (and which had been the subject of the crowd's protest in the first painting in this series).

verbal description of hotspot location: Squire Timothy Parti-tool  & Porter & Peddler, just outside the bay window
annotation text 0: Squire Timothy Parti-tool, Esquire, the richly dressed and pointedly politically named gentleman standing in the courtyard of the Royal Oak, is one of the candidates in the election. He is arranging to make a purchase from the peddler at his feet, which will be intended to secure the political support of the women above him on the balcony, from which he has apparently just descended (having left his hat there).  A porter has also just delivered stacks of printed election papers to Squire Parti-tool. Hogarth is implying through his name that he is a ‘tool’ of the Tory Party, and will do whatever he is told to do to win the election. It will be his job to distribute the paperwork piled at his feet to secure votes.
annotation text 1: Eighteenth-century contested elections harnessed the power of the press to reach voters and non-voters alike. Hogarth here introduces us to the ‘paper wars’ that had become a common feature of mid-century contested elections. Convenient rips in the packaging of the printed paper in this image tell us about the papers that Sir Timothy is receiving. The top stack of printed papers in the picture is a playbill, supposedly advertising a play to be held ‘AT PUNCHES THEAT[RE] …. IN THE ROYAL OKE YARD’. This is unlikely to be an actual play; it is more likely to be a coded invitation that will be pasted up around the town, inviting voters to come to the Royal Oak at a certain time and on a specified date to receive cash for their votes. As such, it suggests that the image of Punch throwing money at the voters, in the banner above Squire Parti-tool’s head, will be translated into reality.  The text on the lower stack of papers reads ‘Sir Your Vote /... & Interest’. These are canvassing cards. They will be neatly printed and include the names of the candidate (or candidates, if two are running together), a polite request for the voter’s votes, and possibly a design or election slogan. They will be given to voters and/or left with voters’ families when candidates and election agents go door-to-door to canvass for votes.
annotation text 2: By the middle of the eighteenth century, contested elections created employment for hack writers and supportive printers as the campaigns produced reams of printed paper. In addition to reporting candidates’ election speeches and the daily state of the poll during the polling itself, printers supplied candidates with canvassing cards that could be left with voters to request their votes and tally tickets for food and/or drink for those voters who had already promised their votes. They also printed scores of satirical election ballads and poems, and actual and fake advertisements and playbills that could be put up around the town.  A really heated election could prove to be an excellent business opportunity for an ambitious local printer: the long campaign leading up to the 1754 Oxfordshire election, for instance, saw the founding of the longstanding local newspaper, Jackson’s Oxford Journal.

verbal description of hotspot location: Ladies on Balcony
annotation text 0: The two stylishly dressed women on the balcony are being bought trinkets from the peddler below by Squire Timothy Parti-Tool in an effort to secure their support and influence in the election.
annotation text 1: While women were not prevented by law from voting in the eighteenth century, they did not vote by custom, even in the 29 English boroughs where they could technically have qualified for the vote. This, however, does not mean that they were uninvolved in politics, or in elections. Both women in the picture are sporting blue (or purple) ribbons and cockades, telling us that they too are supporters of the Old Interest Tories.
annotation text 2: In the eighteenth century there were a variety of different qualifications for voting. In 29 English burgage boroughs, the vote was tied to the ownership of burgages  — small pieces of land that had been granted the vote from ‘time immemorial’. In these boroughs, the sex of the voter was unimportant; ownership of the property conferred the vote. Consequently, those women who owned burgages — and there always were a number — had the right by law to vote in the eighteenth century. In practice, however, they did not vote; they appointed male proxies to vote for them. These might be male family members or political appointees.  As elections in burgage boroughs were often very hard fought, women who were burgage-holders could be canvassed repeatedly and offered substantial treats and bribes in order to secure their support and the appointment of a proxy who would vote for a specific candidate. In other kinds of constituency women could also be the object of canvasses and treating because they were expected to influence the men in their families who did have the vote.
annotation text 3: For further information on women’s electoral involvement, see: ‘Women as participants in elections’: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/woman-as-voters-and-participants-in-elections/   For women’s use of fashion to make a political statement, see this short essay on ‘Fashion and Faction’: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/fashion-and-faction/

verbal description of hotspot location: Prominent location for note marker since this is the introductory annotation. Top-left of painting?
annotation text 0: The third painting in the series is called ‘The Polling’ and shows the actual voting. As in the previous painting (but not the first or fourth), Hogarth sets the action in an attractively rural location, which would no doubt be peaceful were it not for the hurly-burly of the election. Voting at eighteenth-century elections was usually took place over several successive days, until all the voters and ‘polled’. It was done publicly, until an Act in 1872 introduced the secret ballot. In this painting, Hogarth shows supporters of both parties coming to vote, while other interested parties look on, challenging the voters or discussing the election. Press ‘play’ to hear from some of them.

verbal description of hotspot location: on roof of hustings
annotation text 0: Hustings were temporary wooden structures, usually made up of an elevated and roofed platform, as here. They were where voting took place during eighteenth-century elections.
annotation text 1: Hustings were erected in public places like town market squares because elections were always theatrical and drew a crowd, but also because voting was a public activity and voters needed to be seen and heard giving their votes. The candidates, their election agents, their friends, and various other voting officials squeezed on to the hustings. Voters came up the stairs to give their votes. Crowds of voters and non-voters, including women and children, gathered around the hustings. They came to hear the candidates give their speeches at the beginning and end of every day’s polling, and to watch the voters give their votes. There was no secret ballot in the eighteenth century. Voters had to state who they were voting for — out loud — in front of officials and the crowd, and have it recorded.
annotation text 2: The hustings brought politicians face-to-face with voters and the result could be literally riotous. Each candidate and his supporters would arrive at the hustings in the morning by around 9 a.m., before the voting started about 10 . The processions were theatrical and colourful, with flags and banners flying, bands playing and people bedecked with ribbons and cockades in the candidates’ colours singing election songs. At the end of the day, when the polls closed about 4 or 5 p.m., the processions would form again and the candidates, accompanied by their supporters, and serenaded by their musicians, would lead their processions to their respective headquarters (usually a local tavern, or the house of an important supporter), where there would be more speeches.    Eighteenth-century crowds were not particularly polite and elections were exciting, noisy, and drink-fuelled community events. They were also made up of groups of people who supported the opposing candidates. To keep the peace, candidates hired local men to serve as stavesmen , or special constables. They had staves (or bludgeons that they could use to protect the candidates in case of a riot, or to break up fights in the crowd. (Note that Hogarth has included a number of staves resting alongside the hustings at the bottom right of this image, as a reminder.) While not everyone could vote in the eighteenth century, anyone could heckle. Candidates were often judged on how well, or how wittily, they dealt with being interrupted. It was customary practice for the candidate who was in the lead at the end of a day’s polling to give the first speech when the polls closed for the day. Usually candidates thanked their supporters and encouraged more votes for the following day, but if a candidate said something was seen as disrespectful of the voters themselves, the result could be an immediate riot, as was the case in Bedford in 1830: see https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/bedford-1830-riot-and-respectability/
annotation text 3: For further information on who could vote in the eighteenth century, see: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/wp-content/themes/ECPPEC/src/js/who-could-vote/     For further information on processions and pageantry in eighteenth-century elections, see: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/processions-pageantry/.

verbal description of hotspot location: On the clerk requiring the oath, in the middle of the painting.
annotation text 0: In order to vote in an election or referendum in the UK today, you need to meet the requirements to vote and then register to be added to the official electoral register. In the eighteenth century, there was no official electoral register, so voters could be asked to take an oath stating that they had the right to vote and another to assert that they had not been bribed. Here a voter is placing his hand on the bible to swear and being offered a quill pen perhaps to sign his name.
annotation text 1: There were several oaths that candidates could require prospective voters to swear before voting in the eighteenth century. Of these, the Freeholders’ oath was meant to ensure that voters met the property qualification to vote in county elections: they had to own or lease land to the value of 40 shillings (or £2). The Bribery oath, which was often demanded in particularly heated elections, where treating had bled over into bribery and corruption, required voters to swear that they had not been bribed in any way and that they were casting their votes independently.  Oath-taking was a serious business in the eighteenth century. It required voters to speak the truth before God, with one hand on the Bible. It also had serious legal implications: being prosecuted for lying under oath — the crime of perjury — could result in fines ranging from £20 to £500 (multiply by 60 to get a modern equivalent). For many voters, this was much more than they earned in a year. Perjurers could also be sent to jail.
annotation text 2: The Oxford Journal of 6 April 1754 had run features on the oaths voters could be asked to swear, particularly the Freeholders’ and Bribery oaths. The Freeholders’ oath required the voter to swear that he held a freehold worth 40 shillings annually. The penalties  for lying were imprisonment for six months, a £20 fine and possibly a stint in the pillory (the stocks). The fine for lying on the Bribery oath was far steeper — a £500 fine and permanent disenfranchisement.
annotation text 3: For further information on contested elections, see: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/contested-elections/ For further information on controverted elections, where charges centring on qualification to vote, or on bribery, were often used to disqualify voters: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/controverted-elections/  For further information on bribery in 18th century elections, see https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/bribery/

verbal description of hotspot location: On the queue of voters climbing the stairs
annotation text 0: In this image, Hogarth is satirizing the electoral process through his depiction of the voters coming up the stairs to vote. Each is shown as being incapable to swear the necessary oaths and make independent choices when voting, either through their physical or mental impairment. At the top of the stairs, Hogarth has painted a voter with learning disabilities who has apparently been carried to the hustings by a man, standing behind him, whose legs are shackled, suggesting he is a prisoner. The orange cockade dimly visible by the feet of the seated voter suggests that, had he been capable of making up his own mind, he would have voted for the New Interest Whigs; however, he is being told how to vote by the shackled prisoner who wears an Old Interest Tory blue cockade. Next comes another voter who has to be carried to the hustings. He is evidently ill, or perhaps even already dead. Following him is a blind voter, being led up the stairs. He wears blue cockades on his hat and on his coat, but an orange ribbons seems to have been attached on top of the latter, implying that someone has taken advantage of his disability to trick him, and that he will not be able to vote as he chooses. Behind him is a man on two crutches who, it seems, may not be able to vote at all because he won’t be able to climb the stairs.

verbal description of hotspot location: On one of the flags
annotation text 0: Eighteenth-century elections were colourful affairs. Each candidate, or pair of candidates, was represented by a colour and that colour was used for flags, banners, ribbons and cockades. In this image, the flags on the hustings display the colours used by the two sides in the Great Oxfordshire Election of 1754: the Old Interest Tories were blue; the New Interest Whigs were orange.
annotation text 1: The use of specific colours gave candidates and their supporters a collective visual identity. It made them easy to identify in election processions and in crowds at the hustings. If you look at the seriously ill voter who is being carried to vote in this painting, you will see that he is wearing an orange cockade on his hat. As a result, anyone seeing him would know that he was going to vote for the New Interest. Hogarth’s print of this painting was monochrome of course, meaning that the electoral colours could not be represented. Interestingly therefore he chose to pin a ribbon with the words ‘TRUE BLUE’ to this same character’s hat.

verbal description of hotspot location: On the solider, bottom right
annotation text 0: Hogarth meant viewers of his painting to conclude that the most honest, worthy and patriotic voter in the picture was this veteran, dressed in his red regimental coat and with his sword hanging from his belt. He is a triple amputee who has clearly served his country valiantly in the wars. Yet he is having his ability to his cast his vote questioned by the clerk. He has lost his right hand and cannot physically place his hand on the Bible, as required, while swearing his oath. Two lawyers, one representing each party, are arguing about whether the soldier’s votes should be accepted.

verbal description of hotspot location: On/ near the staves/bludgeons, bottom right
annotation text 0: It was not unusual for fights, or even riots to break out during elections. As there was no police force in the eighteenth century to keep the peace, candidates often hired local men to act as special constables. These men were armed with wooden bats or bludgeons, or poles called staves, and were known as bludgeon-men or stavesmen. In this picture, Hogarth has pointedly included a number of staves, leaning against the hustings, to remind the viewer of the possibility of electoral violence.
annotation text 1: For an example of an 18th century bludgeon, see here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/31257118-e5d8-417c-ab51-626a2006aaa9/  For further reading about violence and riot in 18th century elections see  Violence and Riot: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/violence-and-riot/

verbal description of hotspot location: Near Britannia's coach and coachmen
annotation text 0: Britannia, a female warrior usually shown seated with trident and shield, has been used as a personification of Britain since Roman times. Hogarth is here is using the symbolism of the broken-down state coach carrying Britannia, and the cheating coachman and postillion, who represent the country’s leading politicians, to argue that ‘Britain is broken’ and that British politics is corrupt and needs to be reformed. It is an argument that can still be heard today.
annotation text 1: The coach, with its broken axle and its image of the Union flag on the door, symbolises the state. The white Hanoverian horses, representing the monarchy, are pulling hard, but unable to right the coach. The female passenger, who is trying futilely to catch the attention of the coachman and postillion, represents Britannia, the symbol of Britain itself.  The coachman and the postillion, who are playing cards and cheating (note that one is hiding a card behind the other’s back), represent the leading politicians in the House of Commons. They are oblivious to the breakdown of the state and unable to root out the corruption because they are too self-interested and corrupt.
annotation title: Britannia and the state of the nation

verbal description of hotspot location: On/above/below the crowd on the bridge
annotation text 0: The supporters of the New Interest Whigs (with orange flags) and the Old Interest Tories (blue) meet on a bridge. Violence ensues and a horse and carriage is about to plummet off the bridge.
annotation text 1: The scene references a tragic encounter that took place on Magdalen Bridge in Oxford at the end of the Oxfordshire election of 1754. A New Interest Whig procession had left the hustings and was crossing the bridge when accosted by a violent, mud-slinging crowd. In the midst of the melée a New Interest Whig supporter, Captain Turton, pulled out his pistol and shot into the crowd. This resulted in the death of a chimney sweep.  The Coroner, who was an Old Interest Tory supporter, subsequently charged Captain Turton with wilful murder. The New Interest Whigs were in a quandary, as they feared that Turton would be condemned to death if he went to trial in Oxford, but equally that he would be lynched by the mob if he was found not guilty. In the end, neither result obtained, as Turton fled Oxford and never stood trial.

verbal description of hotspot location: Between the two candidates who are seated on chairs at back of hustings
annotation text 0: The candidates are seated at the back of the hustings on raised chairs. The Old Interest Tory is on the blue side (denoted by the flag above); the New Interest Whig is on the orange side.
annotation text 1: During elections, candidates were expected to attend the hustings daily. The Old Interest Tory candidate is a portly man who loves his venison and claret. He is hot and sweaty, and looks uncomfortable. Like most elite men of the time, he has shaved his head and is wearing a powdered white wig. He is captured scratching his head while looking at a ‘Bill’ he is holding. Presumably this account of the cost of his election campaign has added to his discomfort. What is encouraging for him, though, is that there is a crowd of blue-cockaded voters drinking on his side of the hustings: his investment in treats and bribes appears to have been successful.  The New Interest Whig candidate seems to have been less successful. He is seated quietly, watching the scene, with his hands on his cane. A man in a red coat below him has drawn a comic a sketch of him and is showing it to two guffawing onlookers.
annotation text 2: Unlike modern elections, where there is only one candidate per seat, almost all eighteenth-century seats elected two candidates. Exceptions included the City of London which was represented by four MPs, and the seats of Oxford and Cambridge universities, which elected only one candidate each. The most prestigious eighteenth-century elections were for the counties (or ‘shires’, such as Oxfordshire). MPs who were elected in county seats were frequently referred to as ‘knights of the shire’ in reference to the elevated status of their seats. Not all of these men actually were knights; many were simply the representatives of the most important landowning families in the area. As elections were expensive and exhausting undertakings in the eighteenth century, candidates often avoided holding elections by agreeing to share the representation between the two leading families: one MP each in a given constituency. Contested elections occurred when challengers emerged who were unwilling to accept the established representation and stood for election individually, or with another candidate as part of a joint package.
annotation text 3: A long, hard-fought election contest could be extremely expensive in the eighteenth century. Preparations for the county election in Oxfordshire began at the end of 1752, and campaigning extended until the election in April 1754. It was, as a result, reputedly the most expensive election of the first part of the eighteenth century. It cost each side c.£20,000 (that’s just over £4 million per side in today’s money).

verbal description of hotspot location: On/near the ballad singer
annotation text 0: Ballad-singers — frequently poor women — scraped a living by going around the streets of eighteenth-century towns and villages selling (and singing) songs. Election ballads, which put new words to popular, well-known songs, were a regular feature of contested elections.
annotation text 1: Election songs were varied. Some were patriotic and celebratory drinking songs; others were written about specific elections, and praised, mocked, or criticised the candidates or their supporters. Yet others were scurrilous and full of sexual innuendo. They could function like party political advertisements today, and could also be a way to spread 'news' about what was going on at an election. Because they could be sung and recited,  you didn't have to be able to read to understand what they said. The ballad singer here is on the Old Interest Tory side of the hustings, where she has gathered a small clutch of listeners. The ballad in her hand, and also in the hands of the men on the hustings who have bought a copy, features the image of a gallows and is meant to be a humorous rendition of ‘The Gallows will Redress our Wrongs’. Given the smiles on the faces of the Old Interest supporters reading the ballad, the words are presumably mocking or attacking the New Interest Whigs.
annotation text 2: Eighteenth-century elections generated many ballads.
