After elections were over they were frequently gathered together with other publications that had been generated by the election — poems, letters, adverts, mock playbills, newspaper reports, poll results, and so on — and published and sold as commemorative volumes. Several were published for the Oxfordshire election of 1754. For more information on the print culture of elections, see https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/features/the-print-culture-of-elections/

verbal description of hotspot location: Prominent location as intro to painting; on left as with others
annotation text 0: This final painting in the series is entitled ‘Chairing the Member’. It depicts the triumphal procession at the end of an eighteenth-century election, when the winning candidate(s) were carried through the centre of the town by their supporters on elaborately decorated chairs. While chairings were generally colourful, music-filled, festive occasions, involving children as well as adults, they could also be violent, particularly if an election outcome was in doubt. In this picture, Hogarth is emphasising the violence and disorder of the crowd, and calling into question the stability of the state itself, as each of the three main buildings represented in the image — the lawyer’s residence representing rule of law on the left, the rather plain and stolid town hall in the centre back representing civic administration, and the church tower on the right representing the established (Anglican) church — are all being bypassed by the political procession. What should be the stabilising forces of law, state and church are having no influence on the people, who the election has incited to corruption and violence.
annotation text 1: Hogarth shows a moment when the candidate is about to be literally 'overthrown'. He is using the imminent toppling of the Tory candidate to indicate the instability of his victory and to foreshadow his eventual formal ‘unseating’ by the New Interest Whigs who, in the 1754 Oxfordshire election, challenged the outcome of the election and, after six months of hearings in front of a Whig-dominated parliament, succeeded in overturning the Tory victory and having their New Interest Whig candidates declared elected instead. Hogarth is suggesting that the electoral system is corrupt from start to finish as even the outcome of the vote can be reversed.
annotation text 2: In reality (as opposed to Hogarth's painting), while some chairings were violent, others were peaceful, festive occasions that involved voters and non-voters alike, as spectators and participants. George Canning’s peaceful chairing in Liverpool at the end of the 1820 election provides an example of the colourful and noisy spectacle that could follow even a demanding contested election. As was often the case, his chairing procession was led by children: by about ‘40 fine-looking boys, pupils at the Royal Liverpool Institution’, marching two-by-two. They carried three ‘beautiful silk flags’, each bearing loyal inscriptions. Following them was a group of men carrying ‘a quantity of colours’ [i.e. flags or banners]. These were likely to have been the stavesmen or bludgeonmen who had been employed as special constables through the election. After them came two of Canning’s most important local supporters mounted on horseback. They led a group of gentlemen, walking four abreast, ‘with colours before and behind’. Next came a musical band and then a parade of the tradesmen supporting Canning —‘Shipwrights, Ropers, Smiths, Riggers, Painters, Joiners, and various other trades, with appropriate dresses and insignia, and colours between each group’. Another band of music followed them, preceding — finally — George Canning himself, seated on a ‘very lofty and magnificent’ chair, ‘profusely adorned with the most splendid and costly ornaments of every description’, which had been mounted on a cart (presumably for ease comfort, and visibility), Officers and men of the local militias, playing drums and fifes, brought up the end of the procession. (Source: 'The Squib Book, Being an Impartial Account of the Liverpool Election, March 1820'… (1820), pp.129–30).
annotation text 3: Explore surviving examples of the chairs for election chairings here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/11047905-dba7-4e12-a582-2b23ed0c1873/, and here https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/5fb91209-37fb-4fe3-8642-0469f5c20b30/]. For a watercolour drawing that shows just how extravagant these ‘chairs’ could be see here https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/50ab8eac-9c98-4e0e-8661-8df5e5c1fad3/.

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above the goose
annotation text 0: A goose flies over the Old Interest (or Tory) politician who is about to fall from the chair. This echoes some famous battle paintings, such as Charles Le Brun’s 'La bataille d'Arbelles', in which an eagle flies above Alexander the Great as an emblem of his majesty. That it's a common farmyard goose that flies overhead here is Hogarth's satirical comment on the candidate's complete lack of dignity and his foolishness. (As Samuel Johnson noted in his famous dictionary, geese in the eighteenth century were ‘proverbially noted, I know not why, for foolishness’.) Hogarth is also perhaps using the goose to pass judgment on the folly of the chairing ceremony as a whole (and by extension the election itself), and to suggest that the Tory candidate is himself a ‘goose’ who will do nothing but ‘cackle’ once in parliament.

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above the soldier at the bottom left of the painting
annotation text 0: The soldier, a New Interest Whig supporter judging by the orange cockade in his hat, has taken off his red uniform coat and shirt, presumably in order not to damage them while fighting the Tories. His head is bandaged as a result of his fighting, and his sword (lying nearby) has been broken. It seems as though all he has received in payment for his services is the quid of chewing tobacco which he has in his hand.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or above the thresher in the white shirt
annotation text 0: A thresher, who would ordinarily use the flail he is swinging to separate cereal grains from husks and straw, and who supports the Old Interest (or Tory) candidates, is involved in a confrontation with a sailor, who supports the other party in the election. It is his flail that, by striking one of the chair bearers, will be the cause of the candidate's fall.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or above the thresher in the blue jacket
annotation text 0: Although he has his back to the viewer, this figure was meant be identified as a sailor by his blue jacket, tricorne hat and his wooden leg. He wears an orange cockade in his hat associated with support for the New Interest (or Whig) party, and is involved in a confrontation with a thresher who supports the Whigs' opponents.
annotation text 1: Explore a bludgeon, used in election rioting, here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/31257118-e5d8-417c-ab51-626a2006aaa9/].

verbal description of hotspot location: on the town hall in the background of the painting
annotation text 0: The town hall symbolises civic administration and government, but it is clear that the authority and good order it represents is being disregarded by the rival electoral factions. The building itself is plain and modern in style (for the 1750s), with sash windows and a cupola containing a bell that stands silent - as if stilled by the raucousness of the procession passing through the street.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the house on the left of the painting, near where it's unfinished.
annotation text 0: This red-brick building is apparently still being constructed, or has fallen into ruin. What has been built is a mix in terms of style, with a Palladian window (sometimes called ‘Venetian’ or ‘Serlian’) above a door that has been ornamented with Chinese-style fretwork. The vogue for ‘Chinoiserie’ peaked in the mid-eighteenth century, and Hogarth includes it as a satire of provincial attempts at be fashionable. In Hogarth’s engraving of this painting, the figure just visible in the upstairs window is identified as a lawyer because the document hanging out of the window has the word ‘Indintur[e]’ written on it.
annotation text 1: An indenture was a formal legal contract that set out specific rights and obligations between two or more individuals. In the eighteenth century, the paper on which indentures were written was perforated or indented (cut zigzag) and cut in half, so that the two sides had to be fitted together to make the paperwork (and the contract) whole. Hogarth is suggesting here that the social contract between the state and the people is itself faulty and in need of correction.
annotation title: An unfinished house and its inhabitants

verbal description of hotspot location: on/above the cooks going into the house on the left
annotation text 0: A procession of servants or cooks is taking food into the house where the New Interest (Whig) elite is going to dine. One servant (dimly visible) has already entered; the next is thin French cook with a long ponytail; then comes an elegant waiter in a blue coat (with an orange cockade in his hat, like the others). Last comes a sturdy female cook, more stereotypically English and rustic than the others, perhaps carrying the traditional patriotic dish: roast beef. Hogarth is satirically suggesting that the Whig elite prefers fancy French foods (and perhaps French politics) to the solid, healthy fare of Old England.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the chap with his head in the barrel
annotation text 0: This figure has his head in a beer barrel, but interpretations differ as to what Hogarth might mean. Perhaps he is depicting a cooper (a barrel-maker) who is trying to find and fix a leak in a barrel (reflective of Hogarth’s belief that the state was in need of repair); or perhaps he is portraying the crude alcoholic excess of the election which has driven a man to put his head in the barrel to lick up the very last drops of beer he can find. Or both. In either case, more beer is on its way, as the two men just behind are carrying another full barrel of beer.
annotation text 1: Beer was the most popular drink for community events such as chairings. It came in barrels  and would have been supplied free to the crowd, paid for by the winning candidates.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the shadow on the wall of the town hall
annotation text 0: In most elections before 1832, two candidates were elected to represent a constituency in Parliament (whereas today, it is one). Here, the shadow of the second victorious Old Interest (Tory) candidate, also being carried in a chair, is being cast on the wall of the town hall.

verbal description of hotspot location: on the mob of people emerging into the scene from the left, mostly with blue cockades
annotation text 0: Most of the members of chairing procession are Old Interest (Tory) supporters, celebrating their apparent victory. They wear blue cockades or blue liberty-caps, and one carries a blue banner labelled ‘Old Interest’ (in Hogarth’s engraving, this was amended to ‘True Blue’). Many of them have staves or bludgeons, and one carries what appears to be a death mask on a pole to which has been pinned the orange cockade of their opponents – as if to assert, or threaten, that the Whig campaign has been killed off. Some of the Old Interest supporters carry meat cleavers and bones, indicating that they are butchers by profession, but also suggesting the potential for violence and even death.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the woman wearing an orange cockade about to strike a man
annotation text 0: There is at least one New Interest (Whig) supporter in the crowd: a woman with an orange cockade on her bonnet. She is beating her Old-Interest-supporting husband (note the blue cockade in his black hat), who has come out to support the chairing and now cowers before her. In Hogarth’s engraving of the painting, the pair of shears or scissors that are attached to his belt, and the lengths of material that hang around his neck, are more clearly visible, indicating that he is a tailor. Husbands and wives did not always agree politically of course. But in portraying this wife beating her husband, Hogarth was exaggerating for effect the common eighteenth-century concern about ‘petticoat rule’ in politics — in other words, that women, though not voters themselves, had huge influence over their husbands’ votes, sexually, verbally, or — as here — physically.
annotation text 1: Hogarth may also have included this grey-haired, New-Interest-supporting woman to make a satirical comment about the 1754 Oxfordshire election, and specifically about the political involvement of Lady Susan Keck, the New Interest’s most committed canvasser and ardent election organiser. ‘A Poetical Description of Mr. Hogarth’s Election Prints in Four Cantos, Written under Mr. Hogarth’s Sanction and Inspection’ (1759) includes the lines ‘When the Grey-Mare proves the better Horse / The Man is mis’rable of Course’, referring to the beating that the Tailor is about to get from his grey-haired wife in the painting (Canto IV, p. 29). In describing the woman as a ‘Grey-Mare’, the writer appears to be referencing a poem in praise of Lady Susan —‘The Gray Mare the better Horse: Or, the Oxfordshire Freeholder’s Choice’— published in ‘Jackson’s Oxford Journal’ (6 Oct. 1753). The poem played on the Old Interest’s accusation that Lady Susan wore the breeches in her marriage and ruled over her husband by suggesting, tongue-in-cheek, ‘That who wears the Breeches may well be a Member’; consequently, the freeholders claimed that Lady Susan was in effect their candidate: ‘Our Choice may seem strange, and we own it is new; / And who do you think is the Man? L[ad]y S[u]e.’

verbal description of hotspot location: On or near the chimney sweeps on the right
annotation text 0: These two young chimney sweeps, although of course they were not eligible to vote, wear blue cockades, indicating support for the Old Interest (Tories). They are covered in soot, although some commentators have suggested that Hogarth wanted them to be recognisable as member of England’s growing Black population, like the servant further along the churchyard wall. One of the chimney sweeps is urinating on the monkey below. The other is placing a pair of spectacles (perhaps made of gingerbread, commonly sold at fairs and entertainments) on a skull. Together with the skull and crossbones, a stone book makes an unusual sculpted finial for the church’s gatepost. The symbolism is obscure, but is clearly connected with death. Indeed, in Hogarth’s engraving of the painting, the gun on the monkey’s back has discharged, and the boy holding the spectacles seems about to be killed. As well as highlighting the precariousness of life, Hogarth here is reminding his viewers about the fate of Joseph Holloway, a real-life chimney sweep, at the end of the 1754 Oxfordshire election. When a Tory mob engulfed the carriage of a Whig supporter on Magdalen Bridge, the Tory-supporting Holloway was shot and killed by a Colonel Turton. When Turton was put on trial, he was found Not Guilty.

verbal description of hotspot location: on or near the sow
annotation text 0: To add to the chaos of the chairing, Hogarth has included a sow and her piglets madly careering through the crowd and off a bridge into the river. A woman, who was perhaps bringing them to the water to drink, has been knocked over, either by the escaping pigs or the fight between the sailor and the thresher. You can see her blue-stockinged foot and her hand behind the thresher.
annotation text 1: It was not uncommon for people in eighteenth-century towns to keep pigs, as they could be fed on scraps and provided families with an important source of meat. As a result, the inclusion of the pigs, and their escape, would not necessarily have been surprising to Hogarth’s viewers. Their inclusion here, however, is also symbolic. Not only does Hogarth use the pigs to suggest that everyone here has their snouts in the trough of corruption, but he also is referencing a Biblical story that his viewers would have known: the story of the Gadarene Swine. This story comes from the New Testament, Mark 5: 1–13 and recounts one of Jesus’s miracles. Upon encountering a madman, Jesus orders the demons possessing the man to leave him, transferring them instead into the bodies of a herd of pigs. The pigs then throw themselves over a steep cliff where they drown in the sea. Hogarth’s use of the fleeing pigs, with one of the piglets already in the water, is therefore a hard-hitting comment on what he sees as the disastrous state of the country and the need for a political miracle to restore the British political system.

verbal description of hotspot location: somewherenear the bear, monkey and fiddler
annotation text 0: The veteran sailor, who is involved in the fight with the thresher, has lost his leg to a cannon ball during a battle at sea. Unwilling to beg, he has acquired a dancing bear and a monkey, whose antics he exhibits for a fee. A fiddler, who perhaps plays the jigs to which the prodded bear will dance, accompanies them as they go from town to town. The bear is muzzled, but hungry. He is ignoring the fiddler and trying to eat from the barrel of offal that is strapped on to a donkey whose progress has been stopped by the melée. The man on the donkey, evidently supposed to be Scottish (and who bears a strong resemblance to the musician playing the bagpipes in the first painting in the series) is about either to beat the donkey or to beat the bear, who is helping itself to the offal. The donkey, who is also hungry, is getting its own back on its Scottish master by eating a thistle, the symbol of Scotland. The sailor has dressed the monkey in a military uniform, taught it to ride on the bear’s shoulders and given it a musket. Hogarth is suggesting that when the Scotsman hits either the donkey or the bear, the monkey’s movements will set off the musket, which will then hit one of the two soot-covered, mischievous chimney sweeps above him.

verbal description of hotspot location: On or near the group of three figures behind the church wall, beneath the sundial
annotation text 0: Seeing her husband about to be toppled from his chair has caused the winning candidate’s wife to faint. Her Black maid — perhaps an enslaved woman — has caught her and prevents her from falling. Another servant is holding a silver vinaigrette of smelling salts — an ammonia-based solution, probably made of spirit of hartshorn or sal volatile dissolved in alcohol or perfume — up to her nose to revive her.
annotation text 1: The eighteenth century saw the growth of empire and, with it, British involvement in the transatlantic slave trade. Among wealthy eighteenth-century families, especially those that owned plantations in the West Indies, it became fashionable to have enslaved (or freed) Black men, women, or children as personal servants and footmen. In these public-facing roles, the Black servants acted as visible status symbols, advertising the families’ wealth, their imperial connections and their taste for the exotic. Abhorrent as slavery is to us today, Hogarth’s painting here dates from more than a decade before the beginning of the campaign for the abolition of slavery. His inclusion of the Old Interest candidate’s wife’s Black servant, therefore, is probably not intended as a comment on the institution of slavery itself, but on the taste for luxury and the exotic that Hogarth believed was corrupting society. Here, he is most likely to be making a comment on the imperial connections of the Old Interest candidate and a suggestion that his wealth (or that of his wife), which comes in some way from the trade in enslaved people, has been used to corrupt the voters and secure his victory.
annotation text 2: It has been pointed out that Hogarth, among all eighteenth-century British artists, was the most prolific painter and engraver of Black people. Black Britons feature in all his major satirical sets of paintings, including 'The Humours of an Election' series. In part, this was an accurate representation of eighteenth-century society: it has been estimated that around 15,000 Black people lived in England in this period, about two-thirds of whom were in London. Many were domestic servants, like the woman in this picture, and it became fashionable for aristocratic and gentry families to employ Black pages or maidservants. But the line between servant and slave could be blurred, and sometimes Black servants were denied legal rights and treated as property. In Plate 4 of Hogarth's 'Marriage à la Mode' series (c.1743), for instance, the Black servant who is depicted serving cocoa is as much of an imperial commodity as the cocoa he serves.
annotation text 3: Hogarth’s representation of Black people in his paintings can also be seen as political. His decision to include Black people in his scenes has been seen as a deliberate statement of democratic and egalitarian beliefs; or as part of his satirical challenge to his contemporaries about how they construct hierarchies and unthinkingly define 'civilisation' and 'savagery'. On the other hand, Hogarth has also been seen as presenting stereotyped, racialised Black figures, or of disregarding the realities of the experiences most Black people in Britain faced in fundamentally racist society.
annotation title: The candidate's wife and her Black servant

verbal description of hotspot location: Near or on the sundial
annotation text 0: The text under the sundial is in Latin and reads ‘Pulvis et umbra sumus’, or ‘We are but dust and shadow’. The quotation is from Horace, Ode VII and is part of a wider contemplation on the passage of time, the turning of the seasons, the fall of the mighty, and the evanescence of earthly success. Hogarth here is using the sundial not only to comment on the immediate physical fall of the victorious Old Interest candidate in the image, but also, by the inclusion of the date on the sundial —1755 — that his political fall is forthcoming too. In April 1755, parliament finally declared the outcome of the previous year’s Oxfordshire election, unseating both Old Interest candidates and declaring the two New Interest candidates elected.

verbal description of hotspot location: On or near the group looking out from the window of the building on the left.
annotation text 0: Three New Interest (Whig) supporters laugh as they watch the Old Interest (Tory) victory parade, confident that their own party will ultimately triumph after they challenge the result of the election in parliament. (Indeed, the apparent victory of the Old Interest candidates in the Oxfordshire election of 1754 was ultimately overturned by parliament in 1755.) The figure with his back to us, offering his support to the apparently defeated New Interest party, is thought to be a representation of the Whig Prime Minister, the Duke of Newcastle, identifiable by his blue ribbon of the Order of the Garter.
annotation text 1: Explore a printed text – written by an Old Interest supporter – that attacks how the result of the Oxfordshire election of 1754 was overturned by parliament, here: https://ecppec.ncl.ac.uk/cultural-artifact-explorer/48e8e841-509e-4d01-8df4-69a489194397/
annotation title: New Interest supporters and the Duke of Newcastle

verbal description of hotspot location: On or near the fiddler, bottom right
annotation text 0: The blind fiddle-player is literally leading the whole procession. Even if (strictly speaking) he is probably part of the act involving the bear and monkey, Hogarth also gives him a major symbolic role. With his long grey beard, his brisk marching steps, the no doubt manically jaunty tune he is playing, and his sightlessness, he is conducting the fools who follow him further away from their duty and into greater folly. Probably Hogarth meant viewers to recall the bible parable told in Matthew 15:14 of the ‘blind leaders of the blind’, which teaches ‘If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch’. It was a theme taken up in other works of art, notably Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s famous ‘The Blind Leading the Blind’ (1568), in which the leader of a collapsing procession carries a hurdy-gurdy, another instrument associated with carnival and mayhem among ordinary people.

verbal description of hotspot location: On the candidate being chaired in the middle
annotation text 0: The first of the two successful candidates in the election is being carried through the streets in celebration. Hogarth is said to have based his portrait on a real MP, George Bubb Doddington, a prominent figure in several governments, but known as a political schemer and turncoat. In 1754, Doddington had in fact lost his seat as an MP (for the borough of Bridgwater), but was able to win another (Weymouth and Melcombe Regis).
